TCS-0467.title: Linear-space LZ77 random access
TCS-0467.formal: Given the greedy LZ77 parse with z phrases of a string $S[1..N]$ over an integer alphabet of size at most N, is there a deterministic word-RAM data structure using \(O(z)\) words in total that returns \(S[i]\) for any $1\le i\le N$ in worst-case \(O(\log  N)\) time? Words have $\Theta(\log N)$ bits. A phrase is a new literal or a longest prefix of the unparsed suffix having an occurrence starting earlier in S; overlapping copies are allowed. Space includes the stored parse and all query-support information. The uncompressed string is unavailable at query time.
TCS-0467.answer_criterion: Construct a uniform data structure meeting both bounds for every greedy LZ77 parse, or prove that no such structure exists in the stated model. Linear space measured by a larger grammar or an LZ-End parse does not meet the \(O(z)\) requirement.
TCS-0467.why: I include this because compression is most useful when a small representation remains usable for selective queries. This question asks whether an extra logarithmic storage cost is an inherent price of navigating repeated data or a consequence of converting to a more convenient representation.
TCS-0467.definitions: All asymptotic constants are universal. The model permits standard arithmetic, multiplication, shifts, bitwise operations, comparisons, and indirect addressing on a constant number of words. A copied phrase beginning at b and referring to \(a<b\) is decoded sequentially, so self-overlap is well-defined. Preprocessing may take polynomial time in N; the target concerns final storage and query time, not construction in compressed time. Use \(1+\log  N\) at the smallest lengths.

progress.text: Ganardi, Jeż, and Lohrey show that a straight-line grammar can be balanced to logarithmic derivation depth with only constant-factor size growth. This settles the corresponding logarithmic-access target in terms of grammar size.
Gawrychowski explicitly asks for linear space in the Lempel–Ziv representation and logarithmic-time character access.

Boneh and Gawrychowski obtain deterministic \(O(z_{\mathrm{end}})\)-space random access in $O(1+\log^2(N/z_{\rm end}))$ time for LZ-End. Their introduction retains classical LZ77 random access as open and records $O(z\log(N/z))$-space solutions for it.

context_blocks.text: Lempel–Ziv compression replaces a repeated block by its earlier starting position and length. This can encode a long text with few phrases, but a position inside one copied phrase may lead to another copy, and then another. Random access asks for just one character without expanding the whole text.

The challenge is not that every deeply referenced string is hard. A long run of one repeated character can be accessed immediately once its simple structure is recognized. The target must work for arbitrary mixtures of copied material, where both the reference chains and the phrase lengths vary. Any shortcuts used to navigate those chains must fit in the compressed-space budget.

Converting the parse to a balanced grammar supplies a route to fast navigation, but the grammar can be larger than the original parse by a logarithmic factor. A space bound proportional to that grammar therefore need not be linear in z. Balancing a grammar already supplied as input is a different, solved representation problem.

The July 2026 LZ-End result is close in spirit: it obtains linear space and improved polylogarithmic access for a variant that restricts copy endpoints. Its parameter counts LZ-End phrases. Since the parsing rule and the number of phrases differ, those guarantees cannot be substituted directly for the classical LZ77 target.

TCS-7177.why: Asks for the sharp universal quality of a comparison when sorting with partial information. It connects uncertainty among compatible rankings to an extremal property of every finite partial order.

TCS-7177.definitions: \([n]=\{1,\ldots ,n\}\). A partial order \(\le _{\mathrm{P}}\) is a reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive relation. Distinct x,y are incomparable when neither \(x\le _{\mathrm{P}} y\) nor \(y\le _{\mathrm{P}} x; \mathrm{P}\) is a total order when no such pair exists. A linear extension is a bijection \(\mathrm{L}:[n]\to [n]\) with \(\mathrm{L}(a)<\mathrm{L}(b)\) whenever \(a\le _{\mathrm{P}} b\) and \(a\ne b\). Let \(E(\mathrm{P})\) be the finite nonempty set of all linear extensions, \(e(\mathrm{P})=|E(\mathrm{P})|\), and \(e_{\mathrm{P}}(x,y)=|\{\mathrm{L}\in E(\mathrm{P}):\mathrm{L}(x)<\mathrm{L}(y)\}|\). Equivalently choose L uniformly from \(E(\mathrm{P})\), so the displayed interval requires \(\Pr [\mathrm{L}(x)<\mathrm{L}(y)]\in [1/3,2/3]\), including endpoints. The pair x,y may depend on the entire poset. This is an existence proposition over all finite orders, with no width, height or representation restriction and no algorithmic requirement. Width is the largest size of a set of pairwise incomparable elements; height is the largest size of a totally ordered subset. For context, the balance constant is \(\beta (\mathrm{P})=\max _{x\ne y} \min \{e_{\mathrm{P}}(x,y),e_{\mathrm{P}}(y,x)\}/e(\mathrm{P})\); this card uses \(\beta\) to avoid conflicting \(\delta\) conventions across sources.

context_blocks.text: A partial order records comparisons already known, and its linear extensions are all complete rankings still compatible with that information. The conjecture says that unless only one ranking remains, some unresolved comparison splits these possible rankings into two substantial groups. Neither outcome may leave more than two thirds of them. The distribution is uniform over whole rankings, not over the currently available choices in a stepwise topological sort.

Take three elements with \(a<b\) and c unrelated to both. The three linear extensions are abc, acb and cab. The probability that a precedes c is \(2/3\), while the probability that b precedes c is \(1/3\). No incomparable pair is closer to a half. This small example shows that the universal interval cannot be narrowed to \([1/3+\eta ,2/3- \eta ]\) for any \(\eta >0\). In a total order every pair instead has probability zero or one, which explains the excluded case.

Uniform local choices need not produce uniform extensions. In the same example, choosing randomly between the two initially minimal elements a and c gives cab probability \(1/2\), and gives abc and acb probability \(1/4\) each. Those are different from the required probabilities \(1/3\) each. Fixing the probability space prevents a superficially similar random-ordering question from replacing the conjecture.

Brightwell, Felsner and Trotter prove the weaker universal bound \(\beta (\mathrm{P})\ge (5- \sqrt{5})/10\approx 0.2764\). It already guarantees an informative comparison and improves the earlier \(3/11\) bound of Kahn and Saks. The requested value \(1/3\) is a sharper extremal constant, rather than the first guarantee of any fixed positive balance.

The conjecture is known for substantial classes, including width-two and height-two orders, and orders whose cover graph is a forest. Width limits how many elements can be mutually incomparable; height limits the length of a chain. These are distinct restrictions, and neither covers arbitrary finite orders. The Chan–Pak survey states the general question separately from this collection of positive cases.

Aires and Kahn obtain stronger asymptotic balance under size hypotheses: for example \(\beta (\mathrm{P})\) tends to \(1/2\) when width is at least a fixed positive fraction of the number of elements. Their 2025 paper still states the unrestricted \(1/3\)–\(2/3\) bound as a conjecture. A result for a sequence of sufficiently wide orders leaves narrower and exceptional finite orders uncovered.

Gupta’s July 2026 revision reports an exhaustive verification of the stronger Gold Partition property through fourteen elements, implying the balance conjecture for those sizes. Its arithmetic and archived artifacts are described in the paper; this review did not rerun the census. A verified finite range, however large its enumeration, does not establish the universal statement.

TCS-7177.answer_criterion: Prove the displayed inequalities for at least one incomparable pair in every finite non-total order, or exhibit a finite non-total order for which every incomparable pair has probability outside \([1/3,2/3]\). All probabilities refer to the uniform distribution on its full set of linear extensions.

TCS-7334.title: Strong SetDisjointness conjecture
TCS-7334.formal: Is it true that every static word-RAM data structure for SetDisjointness with space \(S(N)\) and worst-case query time \(T(N)\) satisfies \(S(N)T(N)^2=\widetilde\Omega(N^2)\)? The input is a list of nonempty sets \(S_1,\ldots,S_m\subseteq[N]\) with total size \(N=\sum_i|S_i|\), and a query \((i,j)\) asks whether \(S_i\cap S_j\) is empty.
TCS-7334.definitions: A uniform sequential word RAM has a fixed finite program, word-sized registers and addressed memory cells. Unit-cost instructions are reads and writes, comparisons, branching, addition, subtraction, multiplication, integer division with nonzero divisor, Boolean bit operations and logical shifts. Arithmetic stored in one word is modulo \(2^w\); shifts by at least \(w\) yield zero. Addresses must fit the available word size. All table construction and input-dependent auxiliary memory count; there is no free advice or input-dependent oracle. Randomized programs may generate independent uniform random words. The sets are supplied as lists without repeated elements within a set, with \(m\le N\) and \(N\ge2\). Word size is \(w=\lceil10\log_2(N+2)\rceil\). Restrict attention to \(N\le S(N)\le N^2\), rounding up and padding unused cells if needed. Preprocessing may use arbitrary finite time; all input-dependent information retained afterwards counts toward \(S(N)\). A query reads this static representation and begins without input-dependent private state. Randomized preprocessing and query algorithms are allowed; the answer to each fixed input/query must be correct with probability at least \(2/3\). Space and query time bounds hold for every random outcome. The notation means that, for each admissible data structure, there are constants \(c>0\), \(b\ge0\), and \(N_0\) such that \(S(N)T(N)^2\ge cN^2/(\log(2+N))^b\) for all \(N\ge N_0\). All sizes are measured in words and time in word-RAM steps. Uniform programs and exact empty/nonempty semantics are required; reporting the intersection is another problem.
TCS-7334.why: This conjecture underlies many space-query conditional lower bounds for text indexes, graph oracles and set systems.

TCS-7333.title: Subquadratic-space 3SUM indexing with polylogarithmic queries
TCS-7333.formal: Do there exist constants \(\delta>0\) and \(C\ge1\) and uniform randomized preprocessing and query algorithms such that, for every \(n\ge2\) and \(A,B\subseteq\{0,\ldots,n^4-1\}\) with \(|A|=|B|=n\), the resulting static index uses at most \(O(n^{2-\delta})\) words and answers whether \(z\in A+B\) in \(O((\log n)^C)\) worst-case time? Each fixed query must be correct with probability at least \(2/3\).
TCS-7333.definitions: A uniform sequential word RAM has a fixed finite program, word-sized registers and addressed memory cells. Unit-cost instructions are reads and writes, comparisons, branching, addition, subtraction, multiplication, integer division with nonzero divisor, Boolean bit operations and logical shifts. Arithmetic stored in one word is modulo \(2^w\); shifts by at least \(w\) yield zero. Addresses must fit the available word size. All table construction and input-dependent auxiliary memory count; there is no free advice or input-dependent oracle. Randomized programs may generate independent uniform random words. Use \(w=\lceil10\log_2(n+2)\rceil\)-bit words. A query is \(z\in\{0,\ldots,2n^4-2\}\), and \(A+B=\{a+b:a\in A,b\in B\}\) uses ordinary integer addition without wraparound. Preprocessing time is unrestricted but must terminate almost surely; its resulting representation must always respect the space budget. Randomized queries use fresh internal randomness, and the per-query success probability is over both preprocessing and query randomness for every fixed \((A,B,z)\). Queries read a static representation and cannot carry free input-dependent information across calls. All stored inputs, hash seeds and auxiliary tables count toward space. The constants and programs must be independent of the input and \(n\). A polynomial universe with exponent four avoids the small-universe direct-address case; it is an explicit benchmark regime of the broader indexing question.
TCS-7333.why: This asks whether a quadratic family of potential sums can support fast membership queries without a nearly quadratic representation.

TCS-0318.title: Planar k-set extremal function
TCS-0318.formal: Let \(K_{2}(n,k)\) be the maximum, over sets P of n distinct points in $\mathbb R^2$ with no three collinear, of the number of distinct subsets \(S\subseteq \mathrm{P}\) of size k strictly separable from \(P\setminus S\) by a line. Determine \(K_{2}(n,k)\) up to universal constant factors, uniformly for all integers \(n\ge 2\) and \(1\le k\le \lfloor n/2\rfloor\).
TCS-0318.definitions: Strict separation means that there are real a,b,c with \((a,b)\ne (0,0), ax\)+by<c for every \((x,y)\in S\), and ax+by>c for every \((x,y)\in\)\(P\setminus S\). The objects counted are subsets S, not their infinitely many possible separating lines. Coordinates have no bounded-precision, grid, or random-distribution promise. The target is worst-case combinatorial complexity, not the running time of an enumeration algorithm. A matching bound means an asymptotic expression \(F(n,k)\) and absolute constants \(0<c_{0}\le C_{0}<\infty\) such that \(c_{0}F(n,k)\le K_{2}(n,k)\le C_{0}F(n,k)\) throughout the stated range, apart from finitely many n which can be absorbed into the constants. Bounds must cover k that grows with n. Complementation supplies the remaining values \(n/2<k<n; k=0,n\) each have one subset. This card specializes the original all-dimensions problem to the plane.
TCS-0318.answer_criterion: Determine a positive function \(F(n,k)\) and universal constants \(0<c\le C<\infty\) with \(cF(n,k)\le K_{2}(n,k)\le CF(n,k)\) throughout \(n\ge 2\) and \(1\le k\le \lfloor n/2\rfloor\). Prove the universal upper bound and existence of matching point sets for every parameter pair in Lean. No predetermined formula grammar or closed form is required; a mere restatement of the defining extremum is insufficient. This asymptotic-complexity target uses constant-factor precision, not additive 0.01. A fixed-k result or the halving case alone does not determine the whole function.
TCS-0318.why: A central unresolved counting problem in computational geometry, it controls the complexity of levels and line-separated ranges. Its persistent gap tests the strength of crossing-number methods and geometric constructions, with consequences for output-sensitive and parametric algorithms.

importance.reason: A defining extremal-complexity question for geometric algorithms, already unresolved in the plane and connected to levels, geometric selection, and parametric optimization.

progress.text: Dey proves \(K_{2}(n,k)=O(n k^{1/3})\) for \(1\le k\le n/2\) through a crossing-number argument. The balanced specialization gives an \(O(n^{4/3})\) upper bound.

Tóth constructs planar point sets with \(n \exp (\Omega (\sqrt{\log  k})) k\)-sets for \(n\ge 2k>0\), improving the earlier n log k scale. This remains separated from the upper bound by an unbounded factor when k grows.

Nivasch gives a simpler halving-edge construction improving the constant in the square-root-log exponent. The construction does not produce \(n^{1+\varepsilon}\) halving edges for any fixed positive \(\varepsilon\).

Alonso, López, and Rodrigo improve a linear subtractive term in the upper bound on the maximum number of halving lines for even n, and improve some finite-n bounds. The asymptotic upper exponent remains \(4/3\).
The revised Open Problems Project entry still lists the planar asymptotic gap as unresolved. A search through September 2026 did not locate matching general upper and lower bounds.

TCS-0318.status_note: The June 2025 problem entry retains the gap. The 2024 halving-line improvement changes lower-order terms rather than the exponent. No matching asymptotic bound was located in the status search through 10 September 2026.

context_blocks.text: A line can realize only a small fraction of all choices of k points. The question measures the combinatorial capacity of one linear cut at a fixed output size. For example, when \(k=1\) the separable points are the convex-hull vertices, and their maximum number is n. The difficult regime lets k increase with the input size.

Point-line duality translates changes of a separating line into the structure of levels in a line arrangement. A level tracks positions having a specified number of lines below them. These level bounds recur in geometric selection and in analyses of parametric optimization. Dey’s method also yields bounds for related level structures, convex chains, and parametric spanning-tree problems.

For even n, the balanced case is closely tied to halving edges: segments joining two input points whose supporting line leaves \((n- 2)/2\) of the other points on each side. A halving edge is not itself a separating line, since it passes through input points. The correspondence between k-sets and directed \((k- 1)\)-edges gives \(K_{2}(n,n/2)\) equal to twice the maximum number of undirected halving edges.

The known planar upper bound is \(O(n k^{1/3})\), whereas constructions give \(n \exp (\Omega (\sqrt{\log  k}))\) subsets. In the balanced regime the latter grows faster than n times any fixed power of log n, yet slower than \(n^{1+\varepsilon}\) for each fixed \(\varepsilon >0\). Thus neither a linear bound nor an ordinary polylogarithmic correction to linear growth can describe the worst case.

Sharper finite-size constructions and improvements to the additive terms of halving-line bounds are useful progress. They do not close the gap in asymptotic growth. Keeping this distinction explicit matters here: an improved upper bound may retain the same \(4/3\) exponent in the balanced case.

TCS-6498.title: Dynamic optimality conjecture
TCS-6498.formal: Fix n ordered keys and an access sequence X. In the root-BST model, an access is served by rotations until its key is at the root; its cost is one plus the number of rotations. Let \(\operatorname{OPT}(X)\) minimize total cost over offline executions, allowing an optimal initial tree. Is there a universal constant C such that, for every initial splay tree \(T_{0}\) and every X, \(\mathrm{cost}_{\mathrm{splay}}(X;T_0)\le C(\mathrm{OPT}(X)+n)\)? The additive term allows an arbitrary initial configuration.

context_blocks.text: A balanced search tree guarantees logarithmic time per access, but that worst-case guarantee ignores the sequence. Repeatedly accessing one key, or scanning nearby keys, can be much cheaper if the tree adapts. Dynamic optimality asks for one online rule that exploits every such pattern without being told which pattern will occur.

The benchmark is itself allowed to rotate its tree and knows all future requests. Competing with the best fixed tree only captures access frequencies; competing with a changing tree also captures temporal structure. Splaying uses only local zig, zig-zig, and zig-zag rotations after each access, with no explicit prediction of the future.

For a concrete example, consider a chain on n keys with the requested key at its bottom. The first splay can cost \(\Theta (n)\), whereas an offline comparator can put that key at the root initially. The additive n allowance accounts for this starting discrepancy. Repeating the same request then costs one per access in both trees. A large cost for one badly initialized access therefore does not refute the statement.

The July 2026 preprint bounds splay cost by \(O((\operatorname{OPT}(X)+n) \log  \log  n \cdot  \log ^{2} \log  \log  n)\). Its competitive factor depends only on the number of keys, so the result covers every access pattern; that factor nevertheless grows without bound. A constant bound would be strictly stronger. The theorem is stated asymptotically, with the finitely many small values of n absorbed into constants.

Competitiveness concerns the total cost of a sequence. It does not require every individual access to be cheap, and it does not compare against an arbitrary RAM program with a hash table. Both executions must maintain binary search trees and pay for the specified rotations. Within those rules the offline execution can depend on the complete sequence, while the splay rule reacts only to the current request and tree.

context_blocks.title: Additional source and scope
context_blocks.text: Sublogarithmic competitiveness of splay trees is a weaker quantitative milestone on the way to constant competitiveness. It is preserved as context and is not claimed to imply dynamic optimality.

TCS-6498.why: It asks whether a simple local adjustment rule can match every legal strategy with complete knowledge of the future. The issue is fundamental to instance-sensitive data structures: success would replace a growing competitive penalty by a constant for all access patterns. A counterexample would identify a limitation of splaying that its many separate locality guarantees fail to reveal.
TCS-6498.definitions: Keys are \([n]=\{1,\ldots ,n\}, n\ge 1\), ordered by their integer values. A binary search tree has one node per key, every key in a left subtree smaller than its root and every key in a right subtree larger. A rotation on a parent-child edge exchanges those two nodes while reattaching the intermediate subtree so that the order is preserved. To splay a requested key x, repeatedly apply the following bottom-up rule until x is root. If its parent is root, rotate the edge from x to its parent (zig). Otherwise let p be its parent and g its grandparent. If x and p are both left children or both right children, first rotate p above g and then x above p (zig-zig). Otherwise rotate x above p and then x above g (zig-zag). Each access costs one plus its number of rotations. The tree after the access is the initial tree for the next access. For a finite sequence \(X\in [n]*, \operatorname{cost}_{\mathrm{splay}}(X;T_{0})\) is the sum of these costs starting from \(T_{0}\). A comparator execution may start with any tree, knows X in full, and serves each request by any finite sequence of parent-child rotations anywhere in the current tree whose final root is the requested key. Its cost is the same one-plus-rotations sum. \(\operatorname{OPT}(X)\) is the minimum cost over all such initial trees and executions; it is zero for the empty sequence. There are no insertions, deletions or additional node operations. This root-BST cost convention is the one used in the saved source, with the additive n term accounting for the initial tree.

progress.text: Splaying has logarithmic amortized access cost and stronger guarantees for useful special patterns. These do not establish competitiveness against an arbitrary changing offline tree.
Tango trees give an online BST with an \(O(\log\log n)\) competitive ratio. This result is for a different data structure and does not settle splaying.
The preprint proves \(O((\mathrm{OPT}(X)+n)\log\log n\,\log^2\log\log n)\) total splay cost. Theorem 1 includes the initialization term explicitly. Constant competitiveness remains the target.

TCS-7235.title: Almost-linear-time \((1+\varepsilon )\)-approximation of edit distance
TCS-7235.formal: For every fixed rational \(\varepsilon \in (0,1)\), is there a uniform classical randomized algorithm \(A_{\varepsilon}\) that, on every pair of explicitly given strings of total length \(n\ge 2\), outputs an integer D with \(ED(x,y)\le D\le (1+\varepsilon )ED(x,y)\) with probability at least \(2/3\), using worst-case time \(n^{1+o(1)}\)?
TCS-7235.definitions: \(ED(x,y)\) is the minimum number of single-symbol insertions, deletions and substitutions transforming x into y, with unit cost per edit and zero cost for an equal-symbol match. String symbols are integers in \(\{0,\ldots ,n^{2}+1\}\), stored in arrays, so binary and other fixed alphabets are included. Use a word RAM with \(w=B_{\varepsilon}\lceil \log _{2}(n+2)\rceil\) bits for a fixed sufficiently large integer \(B_{\varepsilon}\); unit-cost operations are random-access reads/writes, comparisons, Boolean operations, shifts, addition, subtraction, multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\) and integer division by a nonzero word. Larger integers require multiple charged operations. Independent fair random bits are allowed. For each fixed \(\varepsilon\) there is one algorithm \(A_{\varepsilon}\), and for every rational \(\eta >0\) there are constants \(C_{\varepsilon ,\eta},N_{\varepsilon ,\eta}\) such that every execution on every pair of total length \(n\ge N_{\varepsilon ,\eta}\) uses at most \(C_{\varepsilon ,\eta} n^{1+\eta}\) operations. \(A_{\varepsilon}\) halts on all inputs and has a finite worst-case bound at each smaller length as well. Constants may depend on \(\varepsilon\) and \(\eta\); the algorithm may depend on \(\varepsilon\) but not on \(\eta\). All preprocessing and output are charged; no advice, preprocessing oracle or input distribution is supplied. Success is required separately for every input pair. There is no additive error or promise that ED is large. Only a numerical estimate is required, not an edit script. No polynomial dependence on \(1/\varepsilon\) or effective procedure generating \(A_{\varepsilon}\) from \(\varepsilon\) is required.
TCS-7235.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation, with all definitions, promises, resource bounds and quantifiers as stated. A conditional result establishes only the explicitly conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-verified proof of the full target.

statement_review.reason: The statement and definitions specify the target, domains, quantifiers and relevant computational model; this is an editorial formulation review, not a formal verification.

selection_provenance.approval_basis: User requested approximately five additions from GPT and five from Claude after the proposal audits.

context_blocks.text: Edit distance captures alignment when one sequence may have inserted or deleted symbols. The near-linear target concerns every input pair and every fixed relative tolerance. It asks whether extremely accurate estimates can be computed with an exponent approaching one, rather than merely improving on the quadratic dynamic program.

The catalogue has two related but different targets. TCS-7220 asks for a \((1+\varepsilon )\)-approximation in \(n^{2- \delta _{\varepsilon}}\) time, with a fixed positive exponent saving for each accuracy. TCS-6624 asks for some fixed constant-factor approximation in \(O(n \operatorname{polylog} n)\) time. The present target strengthens the running-time requirement of the former. Its \(n^{1+o(1)}\) guarantee does not itself promise the fixed polylogarithmic overhead of the latter.

The quantifier over runtime slack is important. For a fixed accuracy \(\varepsilon\), one algorithm must meet \(n^{1+\eta}\) bounds for every fixed \(\eta >0\) once n is large enough. A different algorithm for each \(\eta\), with uncontrolled dependence on \(\eta\), is not automatically such an algorithm. Conversely, this card does not demand a common running-time bound polynomial in inverse accuracy.

Andoni and Nosatzki obtain constant-factor approximation in \(n^{1+\eta}\) time for each fixed \(\eta\). Mao and Rubinstein’s March 2026 approximation scheme moves toward arbitrarily accurate approximation, but its stated runtime is quasi-strongly subquadratic. Those advances concern different points of the accuracy–time tradeoff and do not establish the present joint target.

Purely multiplicative error also controls almost identical strings. On equal strings the successful output must be zero; an additive error term increasing with n would violate the statement. This requirement separates the question from weaker large-distance guarantees. The three cards therefore record distinct accuracy–runtime requirements, with their implications stated separately.

TCS-0468.title: Linear-time LZ77 pattern matching
TCS-0468.formal: Is there a deterministic algorithm that, given a valid LZ77 representation of z phrases of a text T of length N and an explicit nonempty pattern P of length m, decides whether P occurs contiguously in T in \(O(z+m)\) worst-case time? Self-referencing copy phrases are allowed. Symbols are integers in $\{1,\ldots,(z+m)^c\}$ for a fixed constant c. Use a word RAM with word size $\Theta(\log(N+m+2))$, the operations specified below, and \(O(z+m)\) working words. The input is the compressed text and the explicit pattern; all preprocessing is included.
TCS-0468.answer_criterion: Give one uniform algorithm with the stated bounds for every valid input, or prove that no such algorithm exists in this model. The output is one yes/no answer. An algorithm linear in the uncompressed text length, or in a potentially larger grammar representation, does not attain this target.
TCS-0468.definitions: Each phrase is either one literal symbol or a pair \((s,l)\) instructing the decoder to append l symbols copied sequentially from an earlier starting position s in the text. For a phrase beginning at p, require \(1 \le  s < p\); the copied interval may overlap the phrase being produced. Phrase boundaries and references occupy \(O(1)\) words per phrase. No promise of a greedy parse is needed. The RAM has random access, comparisons, addition, subtraction, multiplication, integer division, and bitwise Boolean operations and shifts on a word at unit cost; arithmetic results are restricted to a word. There is no access to a separately stored decompressed text or precomputed index.
TCS-0468.why: This is a basic test of whether computation can follow the compressed input size rather than the size of the object it describes. Settling it would also clarify whether the representation gap between LZ77 and grammars creates an unavoidable algorithmic cost for a fundamental string operation.

progress.text: Gawrychowski gives deterministic \(O(z(1+\log (N/z))+m)\) time for LZ-compressed occurrence detection, including self-referential parses.
Ganardi and Gawrychowski obtain \(O(g+m)\) time when the supplied text representation is a grammar of size g. This resolves the grammar-input version.
Gawrychowski asks whether the Lempel–Ziv version can be solved in time linear in compressed-text size plus pattern length.

No resolution of this precise LZ-input target was located. The source question is specialized here by making the model and input encoding explicit.

context_blocks.text: Ordinary pattern matching scans the text and pattern in linear time. That guarantee can be too expensive for compressed input: a short sequence of copy instructions may describe a text many orders of magnitude larger than the representation. Here the algorithm only has to determine whether an occurrence exists, so a large number of matches does not force a large output.

A match can cross phrase boundaries or occur inside a repeated region. For example, a pattern may start near the end of one copied block and finish in the next. Inspecting each phrase in isolation therefore misses valid occurrences. The challenge is to summarize enough boundary and periodicity information while charging only constant total work per input phrase and pattern symbol.

Grammar compression provides an instructive comparison. Linear-time pattern matching is known when the input is a straight-line grammar, but converting an LZ77 representation to an appropriate grammar can increase its size. The existing grammar algorithm therefore does not immediately give linear time measured in z.

The 2025 seminar question explicitly retains the Lempel–Ziv target. This card fixes the decision version, permits self-references, and charges preprocessing. These choices prevent a reporting cost or an uncharged text index from changing the question.

TCS-6513.title: Constant-factor approximation of the smallest grammar
TCS-6513.formal: Do there exist an absolute constant C and a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, for every explicit nonempty string s, outputs an acyclic context-free grammar generating exactly s whose size is at most $C g^*(s)$? There is one production per nonterminal, one designated start nonterminal, and every right-hand side is a nonempty string of terminals and nonterminals. The dependency graph on nonterminals must be acyclic. Grammar size is the sum of all right-hand-side lengths, and $g^*(s)$ is the minimum such size. The alphabet is part of the input, encoded by integer symbols in {1,...,|s|}.
TCS-6513.answer_criterion: Prove existence of one polynomial-time algorithm with some fixed approximation constant valid for all strings, or prove that no such algorithm exists. A hardness theorem conditional on \(\mathrm{P} \ne  \mathrm{NP}\) should be reported with that assumption. Exact optimization and ratios tending to one are stronger targets than the constant-factor question.
TCS-6513.definitions: Expanding a nonterminal means repeatedly replacing it by its unique right-hand side. Acyclicity guarantees termination, and the start expansion must equal the input string with no extra strings generated. Each terminal or nonterminal occurrence on a right-hand side contributes one unit to size. Runtime is measured in the ordinary binary encoding of the explicit input, not the compressed output length. Constant C cannot depend on the alphabet size, string length, or optimal grammar size. Arbitrarily long right-hand sides are permitted; the size convention is not just the number of productions.
TCS-6513.why: This is a fundamental compression-versus-optimization question: can an efficient procedure recover a representation within a fixed factor of the best hierarchical description? It also supplies a benchmark for compressed-data algorithms, whose costs often depend on grammar size rather than on the original string length.

progress.text: Charikar and coauthors give an \(O(1+\log (|s|/g*(s)))\) approximation and rule out approximation ratios below \(8569/8568\) unless \(\mathrm{P} = \mathrm{NP}\).
Casel and coauthors establish hardness over fixed alphabets of size at least 17 and retain constant-factor approximation as Open Problem 2. The hardness result does not rule out every constant.

references.locator: Sections 1.3, 2.2, and 6.2; Open Problem 2; online 13 November 2020, journal volume 2021

TCS-6513.status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026 using the primary approximation and fixed-alphabet papers, with a search for later results. No general constant-factor algorithm was located. Recent assembly-index work uses additional size conventions and is not treated as resolving this proposition.

context_blocks.text: A grammar can share repeated pieces of a string and then share larger pieces assembled from them. For example, a sequence of doubling rules represents an exponentially long run using only a linear number of rules. This makes grammar size a useful concrete measure of repetitive structure, with a finite optimum that can in principle be found by exhaustive search.

The problem is to choose the shared pieces. Two useful repeated substrings may overlap, and a locally attractive substitution can prevent a better organization at a larger scale. A method that compresses some families extremely well can therefore still have an unbounded ratio to the best grammar on other families. The proposed guarantee must cover every input, not only average compression performance.

Known approximation guarantees depend logarithmically on the ratio between the explicit string length and its optimal grammar size. Hardness rules out sufficiently accurate approximation under \(\mathrm{P} \ne  \mathrm{NP}\), but this does not exclude a coarser universal constant. The space between these two conclusions is the question on this card.

The size measure is essential. Counting productions, binary concatenations, or all right-hand-side symbols gives related but different optimization problems. Stating the measure explicitly also avoids confusing exact binary-alphabet hardness questions with the unrestricted constant-factor approximation target.

TCS-6513.review_note: Individually written from the cited primary sources. The importance assessment is editorial. New preprint proofs have not been independently verified.

TCS-7322.title: Optimal approximation ratio for shortest common superstring
TCS-7322.formal: Determine \(\rho _{\mathrm{SCS}}=\inf\){\(r\ge 1: a\) uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm returns a feasible solution of objective value at most \(r\cdot\)OPT on every shortest common superstring instance}, in the input and output model below.
TCS-7322.definitions: Symbols are integers from \(\{1,\ldots ,\sigma\}\), encoded in binary; \(\sigma\) and all strings are input. Running time is measured on a deterministic Turing machine in the total bit length of this explicit representation. String length counts symbols. Repeated and empty input strings are allowed. For an empty collection, OPT is zero. The output is an explicit string over the input alphabet, and containment means ordinary forward contiguous occurrence without reversal, reverse complementation or cyclic wraparound. All preprocessing is charged. For each fixed ratio r in the defining set, one finite deterministic algorithm and one time polynomial must work on every instance; both may depend on r. The infimum is over these globally uniform guarantees and need not be attained. There is no per-input-size choice of algorithm, advice or free optimization oracle.

context_blocks.text: The target is the infimum polynomial-time approximation ratio. The factor-two algorithmic question discussed in the saved history selects one threshold in this larger numerical target.
Shortest common superstring formalizes assembly of overlapping sequences. The unresolved factor two is an approximation barrier for the problem itself, regardless of the algorithm used.

An August 2026 preprint gives a \(7/3\) approximation. A separate September preprint claims a counterexample to the factor-two guarantee for maximum-overlap greedy. Even if that claim is correct, it concerns a particular algorithm and does not answer the general existence question here.

TCS-7322.why: A long-standing approximation threshold for a basic string-assembly problem with direct algorithmic genomics and compression motivation.
TCS-7322.answer_criterion: Supply a specified real number a and prove in Lean that |\(a- \rho _{\mathrm{SCS}}|\le 1/100\). The proof must certify both a lower and an upper bound for the unrestricted quantity in this card. Equivalently, certified bounds \(\ell\)\(\le u\) of width at most \(1/50\) qualify by taking \(a=(\ell +u)/2\). An exact value with proof of equality also qualifies. An unevaluated copy of the defining extremum, a one-sided improvement, or a numerical estimate without a proved error bound does not meet this criterion. The \(1/100\) tolerance is benchmark acceptance; it does not prove an associated exact threshold conjecture. Any hardness assumption must be stated explicitly; a conditional lower bound establishes only its conditional conclusion.

TCS-6669.title: Breaking factor two for sum-of-pairs multiple sequence alignment
TCS-6669.formal: Does some universal \(\varepsilon >0\) admit a polynomial-time \((2- \varepsilon )\)-approximation for minimum sum-of-pairs multiple sequence alignment with an arbitrary number of input strings and metric substitution/gap costs?
TCS-6669.context:
The constant \(\varepsilon\) must not shrink with the number k of strings. Bounds \(2- q/k\) for fixed q do not settle it. Distinguish sum-of-pairs from column scores and local alignment.

No sum-of-pairs MSA approximation question identified. Prior edit distance concerns TWO strings and running time.
TCS-6669.why: A principal approximation barrier for a core bioinformatics optimization problem, requiring a constant improvement independent of the number of sequences.
